idiom_name: interface port + typed mapper module + schema parse at untrusted seams (zod)
implementation_notes: TypeScript's types vanish at run time, so the boundary is a module plus a parse: the acl/ module exports the domain's own interface (interface OrderPort { place(o: Order): Promise<Receipt> }), the adapter implements it and holds the vendor client, DTO interfaces describe the foreign shape, and a schema library (zod, or io-ts-style decoders) validates the payload before the mapper turns it into domain types. What replaces the classic facade/adapter/translator classes is the interface plus typed mapping functions; the classes are still justified when the adapter holds configuration or the port has several members. Vendor .d.ts declarations do not enforce the boundary - only the module's exports do.
pitfalls: An interface is a compile-time promise: JSON.parse returns any, so without a runtime parse a renamed upstream field becomes undefined that the compiler never flagged.
Type assertions (as LegacyOrderDto) silence exactly the check the seam exists for - parse instead of asserting at the boundary.
Structural typing accepts any object with the right shape, including the vendor's own: keep vendor response types out of the domain's type graph.
Ambient declarations (@types/vendor) pull vendor types into compilation; reference them inside the acl module only, so the import graph stays honest.
